newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metal employers seek non-wage cost cuts.
newsitem.headline: German metal employers seek non-wage cost cuts.

text.p: German metal industry employers will seek to cut non-wage labour costs when they meet IG Metall union officials this week to discuss new wage contracts.

Werner Stumpfe, head of the metal industry association Gesamtmetall, told Handelsblatt newspaper: "The new law must be reflected in the wage contracts that will be negotiated. We want the final package to include the sick-pay ruling and an opt-out close."

At issue is a law passed in September aimed at allowing employers to cut sick pay allowances from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent, a move which would cut about 12 billion marks ($7.80 billion) from German industry's labour costs.

Since the law took effect, employers and the union have been locked in a bitter debate about how it will be reflected in 1997 wage contracts. They agreed to meet near Frankfurt from Monday to Wednesday to discuss their differences.
Germany has some of the most generous sick pay and holiday provisions in the world.
Stumpfe, in an article released ahead of publication on Monday, said a reduction in non-wage labour costs was necessary to halt a dramatic loss of jobs.
IG Metall said on Friday it was quite pessimistic about the chances for an overall wage agreement. "The positions are currently so wide apart," a spokesman said.
Gesamtmetall said the metalworking and electrical engineering sectors had lost about 142,000 jobs between August 1995 and August 1996, according to data from the Federal Statistics Office.

IG Metall has said it would settle for a 1997 real wage freeze in exchange for job protection guarantees, but Gesamtmetall says it could not agree to this unless real reductions in overall employment costs were made.
IG Metall wants Gesamtmetall to make clear its final position on sick pay by October 23, a day before a second day of planned national protests in the sector.
